props.title: Dead Alive
props.initialSlug: A zombie comedy where love meets lawnmower mayhem

sections.content: Peter Jackson's Dead Alive (1992) - originally titled "Braindead" - stands as the goriest zombie comedy ever made. Before crafting Middle-earth epics, Jackson gleefully pushed practical effects to their limits, using 300 liters of fake blood in the legendary lawnmower scene alone. The film follows Lionel Cosgrove battling zombie hordes after his overbearing mother gets bitten by a Sumatran Rat-Monkey. It shares DNA with Sam Raimi's Evil Dead II (1987), cranking slapstick horror to absurd extremes. Both films weaponize household items - Ash's chainsaw hand meets Lionel's whirring lawnmower - while pioneering the splatter-comedy genre.

sections.content: The early 1990s marked peak practical effects in horror comedy, with films like Army of Darkness (1992) and Demons 2 (1986) pushing physical gore and creature work before CGI took over. Dead Alive represents the pinnacle of this approach - every splatter gag, puppet zombie, and mutant creature was achieved through ingenious practical effects by Bob McCarron and Richard Taylor's team. The "mother monster" finale required the largest puppet ever built in New Zealand at that time. SUBHEAD: The New Zealand Splatter Film Movement

Jackson's early films helped establish New Zealand's unique splatter movement. While American horror leaned toward slashers, Kiwi films like Meet the Feebles (1989) and The Quiet Earth (1985) mixed horror with distinctly dark humor and social commentary. This tradition continues in modern films like Deathgasm (2015) and Black Sheep (2006), which maintain the practical effects-heavy approach while satirizing New Zealand culture.
